Bam Adebayo has a plan for slowing Luka Doncic, and he shared it before the Miami Heat headed to Los Angeles. The Heat face the Lakers on Monday night at Crypto.com Arena, the first stop on a five-game West Coast trip.Doncic is averaging 36.2 points in his first five games, which gives Miami plenty to solve. The Slovenian star also scored 37 in the Lakers’ 112-95 loss at Golden State on Oct. 30. The Heat opened 0-4 but have won two straight, and Adebayo kept his message short and simple.Bam Adebayo told reporters on Sunday how Miami will handle Luka Doncic, and the plan is not complicated. “We’re just going to try and make him make difficult shots,” he said. Miami wants Doncic to see two defenders and think before acting, and the goal is to get other Lakers to miss. Adebayo added other teams around the league do the same thing.Miami has the personnel to try it. Adebayo and Giannis Antetokounmpo anchor the Heat defense, and Doncic is also averaging 7.6 assists and 6.8 rebounds, so sending help is not a clean fix. The Lakers were 4-2 before Sunday’s game against Toronto. A win in Los Angeles would give Miami a boost after its 0-4 start and extend its two-game streak.Miami may not need a perfect plan if Los Angeles keeps giving ground when Doncic rests. The Lakers have been outscored 164-119 in the 60 minutes and 41 seconds Doncic has sat across five appearances. The figure leaves out the Oct. 28 game against the Clippers, which Doncic missed with back tightness. The Lakers won it 103-87, and Collin Sexton scored 21.The Warriors game showed the gap. Los Angeles was plus-9 during Doncic’s 37 minutes and 21 seconds and minus-26 over the other 10:39. Golden State’s bench outscored the Lakers’ reserves 50-7, and Sexton went 0-for-6. Austin Reaves had eight turnovers, six of them with Doncic on the floor, and the team gave it away 22 times in all.Coach JJ Redick was direct afterward. “Got to figure the turnover thing out,” he told reporters.With Doncic on the floor, the Lakers have a 130.7 offensive rating and a plus-17.9 net rating. Adebayo’s plan fits that split. Make the star work, then see if the supporting cast can make Miami pay.
Article Summary: Bam Adebayo has a plan for slowing down Luka Doncic. The Miami Heat face the Lakers on Monday night in Los Angeles. The Lakers have been outscored 164-119 in the 60 minutes and 41 seconds the Slovenian star has sat.

Article Title: Virat Kohli has better chance of scoring century than Rohit Sharma: Former India cricketer drops big verdict

Former India batter Cheteshwar Pujara believes Virat Kohli has a better chance than Rohit Sharma of scoring a century in the upcoming ODI series against New Zealand.Pujara feels Kohli's position at number three gives him more time to settle in and build an innings. Rohit, meanwhile, usually has the responsibility of giving India an aggressive start during the powerplay, though Pujara believes his role could change in New Zealand conditions.“The way Rohit bats, he has a role of providing good starts in the powerplay. In New Zealand, maybe that role changes, so he could go for a century. But for Virat, the chances are slightly higher because he bats at number three. His game is more about playing the anchor role. So, for a batsman coming in at number three, scoring a century in the ODI format becomes a bit easier," the former India batter said."The opener’s role is also defined, but in New Zealand conditions, that changes a bit. So, I feel Virat has more chances of scoring a hundred in New Zealand than Rohit,” Pujara told JioStar, as quoted by news agency IANS.Pujara also expects the five-match series to be closely contested. He believes New Zealand could have a slight advantage because India will field different combinations in the first three matches and the last two.While Pujara is backing India to do well in the first three games, he expects the team to face a tougher challenge in the remaining fixtures.“Two-all. In the first three matches, one team is playing, and then, in the last two matches, another Indian team is going to play. So, I think New Zealand have a slight advantage because you aren’t playing the same team in all five matches. I’m still backing the Indian team in the first three matches, as I feel they will do well."The last two matches could be a bit of a challenge, but it will be a hard-fought series. And it rains in New Zealand, so probably one match will be a washout,” he added.

Article Title: Ex-cop among 4 robbers caught as villagers give chase; Rs 36cr bank heist foiled in Maharashtra
Article Text:
The recovered loot of the Jalgaon heist

Jalgaon SP Shrikant Dhivre at the crime spot

Videograb showing one of the robbers fleeing the crime scene





NASHIK: An audacious heist at a nationalised bank in a Jalgaon village ended in dramatic fashion on Saturday, with alert bank employees, villagers, police patils and local cops launching a relentless pursuit that saw all four robbers arrested within hours and the entire loot recovered.The gang had stormed into the bank armed with a firearm, assaulted staff, fired a shot and escaped with Rs 12.3 lakh in cash and 27kg of pledged gold worth Rs 36.4 crore before an extraordinary chase brought their getaway to a halt.Among those arrested is a dismissed police sub-inspector who had recently secured bail in a similar bank robbery case. “Shankar Jasak, once posted in Raigad district police, had earlier been arrested in a bank robbery involving cash and gold in Jalgaon district and was released on bail only a few months ago. All four accused are habitual offenders with criminal records,” said inspector Shashikant Patil, of Jalgaon Taluka police.The robbery unfolded between 2.45pm and 3.15pm at the bank in Bhokar, a village of about 5,000 residents. According to the bank manager’s complaint, business was proceeding normally when four helmet-clad men entered the branch. Their faces were concealed with handkerchiefs. There were no other customers at the branch at the time.Within seconds, one of the men pulled out a firearm and threatened the security guard and a clerk. As he held them at gunpoint, the cashier discreetly pressed the alarm. The move angered the robbers. They rushed at the cashier and rained blows with a wooden stick on him, demanding that the alarm be switched off. The robbers then demanded keys to the strong room. Four employees were tied up with adhesive tape and forced to sit on the floor. When the bank employees resisted, the gang intensified the assault. The robbers even fired a shot at the security guard during the ordeal. The bullet missed the guard and he was not injured.The gang forced the manager and cashier towards the strong room. When the cashier refused to cooperate, another employee was untied and compelled to open it. The robbers stuffed bags with cash from the vault and counters before moving to the gold safe, where they packed mortgaged jewellery into multiple bags.Before fleeing, the gang herded bank employees near a washroom, tied their hands, taped their mouths shut and locked them inside.The escape plan, however, began unravelling almost immediately. Two employees managed to free themselves and rushed out of the bank just in time to spot the robbers speeding away on separate motorcycles. They alerted villagers to the robbery, and themselves set off in pursuit.What followed was a spontaneous village mobilisation.Word spread through Bhokar within minutes. Residents mounted motorcycles, alerted people in neighbouring villages and began tracking the fleeing gang across rural roads. Police patils joined the effort, relaying information and helping block possible escape routes.“My nephew, who has a service centre in the area, called and told me something was wrong inside the bank,” said Sambhaji Pawar, the father-in-law of the local village police patil. “I immediately informed Jalgaon Taluka police. The police station is nearly 30km away, but villagers had already begun chasing the robbers. At the same time, people in neighbouring villages were alerted to block roads and watch for suspicious vehicles. ”“Bhokar is connected by four major roads,” said inspector Patil. “We immediately tightened surveillance and alerted police patils across the area. They gathered local residents and helped seal possible escape routes,” he added.The chase continued for nearly 17km through a network of village roads.The breakthrough came at Diksai village, where villagers intercepted two of the accused just as a police team reached the spot. The two robbers were identified as Ankush Tulshiram Pawar, alias Chavan (25), of Burhanpur in Madhya Pradesh, and Ankush Shravan Chavan (30), of Jalgaon district. Interrogation at the scene yielded vital clues about the direction taken by the remaining robbers. Acting swiftly, Dharangaon inspector Ramakant Gaikwad organised a road blockade, leading to the arrest of the other two accused, Gajanan Pawar (32) of Nashik district and Jasak.Police recovered the entire stolen haul, including all cash and the 27kg of pledged gold, bringing the operation to a successful conclusion within hours of the robbery.Police said the accused have extensive criminal backgrounds. Apart from Jasak’s previous bank robbery case, Gajanan Pawar faces a murder case, while Ankush Tulshiram Pawar has robbery cases registered at Muktainagar and Jamner police stations.Superintendent of police Shrikant Dhivre, who supervised the operation, later felicitated villagers whose swift response and pursuit proved crucial in cracking the case within hours.
Article Summary: Gang stormed into the bank armed with a firearm, assaulted staff, fired a shot and escaped with Rs 12.3 lakh in cash and 27kg of pledged gold worth Rs 36.4 crore. Among those arrested is a dismissed police sub-inspector who had recently secured bail in a similar bank robbery case. All four accused are habitual offenders with criminal records.

Article Title: Learning over drinks: How Bengaluru’s bars and pubs are becoming spaces for intellectual debate
Article Text:
Bengaluru's bars and pubs are evolving into spaces for education and intellectual discussions.

Third spaces for a busy city

Learning beyond the ordinary

A room where ideas can breathe

Finding the right scale





Political and philosophical debates during the french revolution often unfolded in taverns, cafés and pubs. Alcohol consumption was central to social life, and these establishments became spaces where ideas were exchanged and debated. In bengaluru, where alcohol remains a familiar social lubricant, some bars and pubs are now serving a purpose beyond the weekend pub crawl.In a country where education is often associated with academic requirements, grades and cut-offs, a growing number of people are exploring learning for its own sake. Events such as ‘lectures over drinks’ offer an anti-utilitarian approach to education — the kind of learning pursued simply for the joy of discovering something new.“For a city like bengaluru, i think bars and parks are the only third spaces,” say the co-founders of pint of view, shruti sah and harsh sne hanshu, who also founded cubbon reads. “The city works almost around the clock, and a huge part of people’s remaining time is spent commuting between work and home. With the pressure of work and infrastructure that doesn’t always give you enough time or space for yourself, communities like pint of view can give you some time off from active participation.Bengaluru is home to some of the country’s leading institutions in science, the arts and public policy. But the founders of pint of view believe there is a disconnect between these institutions and the wider public. “These institutions produce incredible work, but they can often feel quite gatekept. It can be difficult to simply walk into a lecture at an institution when you need an id card or have to be affiliated with it,” they say. Inspired by the us-based lectures on tap series — and tired of waiting for it to come to india — they decided to create their own version.These are not the conventional classrooms where students once had to ask permission even to drink water during a lecture. Bars are strategic venues for such events: they are centrally located, close to where much of the working population spends time and convenient for those looking to unwind after work with a beer or a cosmopolitan while learning about artificial intelligence, geopolitics, the human brain or almost any subject imaginable.Ronit, an independent filmmaker who has attended lectures over drinks, says the events have helped him meet new people and build connections. “You can watch videos online about different topics that might interest or challenge you. But the offline experience is a whole lot better. You get to ask questions, the speakers respond, and that creates a kind of bond for the duration that you’re in the room,” he says.Another attendee, aditi, draws a distinction between these events and typical classroom lectures. “The speakers are also there because they want to be, not because a job compels them to. They know there’ll be questions from people with diverse backgrounds, so they’re ready for it,” she says.“At brydge, we wanted to go beyond the ordinary events that happen,” say siya pravin sarnaik and atharva atul rampure, the co-founders of brydge, which started intellect on ice.The duo were studying in the uk when they noticed people gathering around niche interests — from specific cuisines to books — something they felt was missing back home. Intellect on ice began in mumbai and has since expanded to bengaluru, delhi and pune. “We felt offline experiences had the potential to be more enriching and that people needed to come together in a more meaningful way. We wanted to create a space to get your thoughts going,” says siya. The events do not follow a fixed format. The team decides which topics to explore, conducts research and then reaches out to people with the expertise and ideas to share. “It’s not a very structured event, but that is the whole point. The experiential economy is booming, and it is in need of infrastructure,” she says.The contrarian debate club, co-founded by school friends sudarshan senthil kumar and srinthan hampi, has also taken intellectual pursuits to bengaluru’s bars and pubs, including woodside inn and big pitcher.The founders wanted to recreate the old british aesthetic of institutions such as the oxford union society. Sudarshan wanted to continue participating in debates after college, while srinthan had been involved in debates and model united nations conferences throughout his life. Together, they wanted to create a space where people could express their thoughts freely and engage in meaningful discussion.“One of the few rooms in bengaluru where no one is going to scream at you,” says sudarshan. He believes good ideas often emerge only after several bad ones have been aired. “To arrive at a good idea, you must go through six or seven bad ones,” he says.Participants are welcome to bring their ideas to the table, as long as they are willing to keep an open mind and listen to others.The club was initially meant to be a gathering of seven or eight friends. But the venue needed a larger crowd for the event to be viable. When the founders invited people on social media at short notice, the idea took off, attracting more than 100 entries.For intellect on ice, one of the initial challenges was finding bars willing to allocate their entire space to a single organiser. Word of mouth, however, proved powerful. The first event, featuring a philosophy professor in a small mumbai bar, took off immediately.“Lectures on tap was also very visible on social media around the same time, so it was the right place at the right time,” says siya. The organisers are taking different approaches to scale.Pint of view plans to expand its lectures to audiences of between 100 and 300 people. It is also organising what it describes as asia’s first lecture festival, a two-day event at jayamahal palace grounds on dec 19 and 20, featuring a series of lectures and an expected audience of up to 5,000.Intellect on ice, on the other hand, plans to remain a more intimate gathering, with between 40 and 60 participants.There is also a shift in the way bars and pubs position themselves, now branching out into more than just drinks. Shane mannas, general manager, big pitcher indiranagar, says that for them, it is about marketing, and people getting to know about the brand. “After such events, we also get repeat guests, who later come with their families and friends as well,” says shane. “To make profits, especially on a usually busy time for us like weekends, we put a cover charge per head, giving the attendees a coupon they can redeem on food and drinks. ” They hold a lot of other events as well, like kitty parties and corporate events.The ticket prices for these experiences range from early bird tickets starting at rs 599 that go live first, going up to rs 1,299. The attendees are mostly people from 25 to 40 years of age, including academics, working professionals, vcs, founders, doctors, lawyers, engineers and cas.
Article Summary: Bengaluru is home to some of the country’s leading institutions in science, the arts and public policy. But the founders of pint of view believe there is a disconnect between these institutions and the wider public. ‘lectures over drinks’ offer an anti-utilitarian approach to education.

Article Title: Ved Rahi, director of ‘Gul Gulshan Gulfam’, passes away
Article Text:
Ved Rahi





MUMBAI: Noted writer-filmmaker Ved Rahi , who directed pictures like ‘Prem Parbat’ and ‘Kali Ghata’, and the popular TV serial ‘Gul Gulshan Gulfam’, passed away at the age of 93 on Sunday.His skills as author and poet drew from a rare command over Hindi and his native Dogri.Ved Rahi was born in May 1933 in Jammu to Mulk Raj Saraf, a pioneering journalist of the state. He attained prominence as a Dogri writer in his hometown, following which he decided to move to Mumbai to test the might of his penmanship.Rahi’s success spanned over 25 films. His fame arose from having written the screenplay or dialogues of movies like ‘Yeh Raat Phir Na Aayegi’, ‘Pavitra Paapi’, ‘Aap Aaye Bahaar Aayi’, ‘Beimaan’, ‘Mome Ki Gudiya’, ‘Sanyasi’, ‘Charas’ and the sparkling ‘Bezubaan’.As his career blossomed, Rahi took the leap into direction with films like ‘Prem Parbat’ (Yeh dil aur unki nigaahon ke saaye), ‘Kali Ghata’ (Shashi Kapoor, Rekha) and recently, ‘Veer Savarkar’ in 2001. Sadly, both ‘Prem Parbat’ and ‘Kali Ghata’ are lost to viewers.Rahi was a familiar name on Doordarshan through the 1980s and 1990s thanks to serials like ‘Gul Gulshan Gulfam’, ‘Meera’, ‘Katha Sagar’, ‘Zindagi’, ‘Ehsaas’ and ‘Rishtey’.His former neighbour at New Sarvottam Society in Irla said, “He stayed here in Andheri for very long. But since many years he was with one of his two daughters. I remember that the print of his movie ‘Kali Ghata’ got destroyed in a fire. He had assisted Ramanand Sagar after he came to Mumbai. Several people from his production house bought flats in Sarvottam society.”Rahi won the Sahitya Akademi Award for his Dogri short story collection ‘Aale’ followed by the Rahul Sankrityayan Award and the Kusumagraj Rashtriya Sahitya Puraskar.He is survived by two daughters Anju Patel and Poonam Advani.
Article Summary: Rahi’s success spanned over 25 films. His fame arose from having written the screenplay or dialogues of movies like ‘Yeh Raat Phir Na Aayegi’ and ‘Pavitra Paapi’

Article Title: In AYUSH admission ‘goof-up’, students in Maharashtra allotted two seats, denied college upgrade
Article Text:
Maharashtra medical admissions: students get duplicate seat allotments (AI image)





MUMBAI: At a time when thousands of NEET aspirants are struggling to secure one medical seat, Deepali Raut* (name changed) has landed two. Both at the same homeopathy medical college in Chinchwad.She is not alone. Several AYUSH aspirants across Maharashtra have been allotted two seats, either in the same college or different institutions, following what appears to be a botched admission exercise that has left some students spoilt for choice and others deprived of a chance to upgrade to better colleges.A senior official of state CET Cell acknowledged the problem, but said little could be done at this stage, given the deadline for completing admissions.The anomalies surfaced in the third merit list released on Oct 30. Under admission rules, candidates allotted seats through the 15% quota administered by the AYUSH Admissions Central Counselling Committee (AACCC) cannot simultaneously claim seats under the 85% state quota.But an Oct 26 order from AACCC changed the equation. Candidates who had failed to secure an upgrade between rounds one and three were permitted to surrender their seats, exit central counselling and participate in the state admission process.The order came too late for the state to accommodate the cancellations before finalising its allotments. The result: candidates appearing on both lists, with some securing two seats.Parent representative and admission counsellor Kailash Tosniwal said the last-minute decision had created confusion and placed candidates in a financial bind. Those who surrender seats allotted through the central quota in private colleges risk forfeiting substantial security deposits. Reserved-category students who give up their state quota seats, meanwhile, could lose the benefit of govt fee concessions at the start of the academic year.But the bigger casualty may be students who were waiting for an upgrade.Candidates holding two allotments must surrender one seat. These seats will now become available in the fourth round, from which students already allotted seats in the first three state counselling rounds are excluded. This creates a peculiar situation: candidates with lower NEET scores who remained unallotted could secure better colleges in the fourth round, while higher-scoring students who accepted seats earlier will have no opportunity to compete for them.Had the admissions been processed in accordance with the original rules, these seats could have been available for upgrades in the third round itself, Tosniwal said, blaming AACCC for the last-minute change. For students who have played by the rules, the consequences may be difficult to accept. Some have two seats to choose from. Others have lost their chance at a better one, said Tosniwal.
Article Summary: Several AYUSH aspirants across Maharashtra have been allotted two seats, either in the same college or different institutions. The anomalies surfaced in the third merit list released on Oct 30. Under admission rules, candidates allotted seats through the 15% quota cannot simultaneously claim seats under the 85% state quota. An Oct 26 order from AACCC changed the equation.

Article Title: 'Ka mau te wehi': Shreyas Iyer's four-word post after India win NZ series leaves fans searching for meaning
Article Text:
Shreyas Iyer (Pic credit: Iyer's X post)

What does 'Ka mau te wehi' mean?

What Shreyas Iyer said after India's series win

NEW DELHI: India captain Shreyas Iyer had a message for his team and fans after guiding the side to a 3-2 T20I series victory over New Zealand, but it was not in English or Hindi. Instead, Iyer chose a four-word Maori expression that left many cricket fans curious about its meaning.Taking to social media after the series concluded on Sunday, Iyer shared a set of photographs from India's campaign, accompanied by the caption "Ka mau te wehi" and a trophy emoji.The unusual phrase quickly caught attention, with fans and cricket followers trying to decipher what the India skipper was attempting to convey through his post.As it turned out, Iyer had picked a popular Maori expression native to New Zealand, the country where India had just completed their international assignment.The phrase, pronounced approximately kah mow teh feh-hee, is an enthusiastic expression of admiration and excitement. It translates to "Awesome!", "That's amazing!" or "Absolutely brilliant!" in everyday usage."Ka mau te wehi" is a Maori kiwaha (colloquial saying or idiom) used to express admiration, amazement or appreciation for something exceptional.While its literal sense is associated with being gripped by awe or wonder, its everyday meaning is closer to saying "Fantastic!", "Outstanding!" or "What a performance!"The word wehi conveys a sense of awe, wonder or an intense emotional reaction.In Maori cultural and performing arts traditions, including kapa haka, it can describe the powerful feeling of being moved or impressed by a performance.Iyer's choice of words was particularly fitting for an Indian side that had managed to secure a series victory on New Zealand soil despite a challenging finish.India had taken an unassailable 3-0 lead by winning the first three matches, but New Zealand fought back with victories in the final two games.Despite the series triumph, Iyer admitted that India could have performed better, particularly after failing to capitalise on a promising batting platform in the final T20I.Reflecting on the seven-wicket defeat, the India captain pointed to the middle-order collapse after his partnership with Ishan Kishan had provided momentum."It was plausible honestly. We could have been better considering the start we got in the middle overs, the way Ishan and I, we created the momentum. And then from there on we lost back-to-back wickets. And then suddenly pressure on the new batsman," Iyer said during the post-match presentation.He also identified bowling and fielding as areas that needed improvement, describing the tour as a valuable learning experience."I think we still could have been better with our bowling and fielding. We were a bit sloppy. But great learning. I think coming overseas, coming to New Zealand, getting to play on such different occasions, different grounds. Yeah, great learning curve," he added.India head coach Gautam Gambhir was particularly impressed with the way Iyer handled the responsibility of leading a relatively inexperienced bowling attack.Praising the captain despite the defeats in the final two matches, Gambhir highlighted the challenges of taking charge of a successful side while providing opportunities to younger players."So, I thought that Shreyas has done a fabulous job with so much inexperience in the bowling lineup because as a captain, you're only as good as how your bowlers or your batters perform. And especially with an inexperienced attack, I think he's done a phenomenal job," Gambhir said at the post-match press conference.The coach also praised the team's overall effort, considering the limited preparation time after the preceding T20I assignment against the West Indies.India's 3-2 series victory, despite losing the final two matches, offered another positive takeaway for Gambhir, who reiterated that the team's aggressive approach would remain unchanged.
Article Summary: India captain Shreyas Iyer posted a message on social media after series win. Iyer chose a Maori expression that left cricket fans curious about its meaning. The phrase, pronounced approximately kah mow teh feh-hee, is an expression of admiration and excitement.

Article Title: Delhi's massive vehicle ban faces its biggest test at the borders: Can enforcement keep up?
Article Text:
(Photo credit: Vinay Gupta/TNN) Delhi is set to implement restrictions on older vehicles that fail to meet BS6 emission standards from entering the city

How Delhi plans to stop non-BS6 vehicles

The tech test

The gaps along the border

Five big challenges for enforcement

Commuters need to know

Beyond the first crackdown

What will determine the success of the ban?

Delhi’s decision to stop older vehicles not meeting BS6 norms from entering the capital brings the focus back to a challenge that is more than announcing restrictions, that of implementing them. With potentially more than 10 lakh vehicles from neighboring NCR cities affected, the success of the move will depend less on the rule itself, and more on how effectively authorities are able to identify, intercept and turn away vehicles at Delhi's numerous entry points.The exercise is on scale. Vehicles from Gurgaon, Faridabad, Noida, Greater Noida and Ghaziabad enter Delhi through a number of busy roads, many of which witness heavy traffic during morning and evening peak hours. It’s neither practical nor sustainable to check each vehicle manually. Even if teams from the traffic police and the transport department are deployed at major entry points, the volume of traffic could quickly overwhelm available manpower.Technology will be important in enforcement, therefore. Cameras using automatic number plate recognition, linked to vehicle registration databases, can help to identify vehicles that do not meet prescribed emission standards.But the system will only work if the cameras cover key entry points, registration records are up to date and enforcement teams can act on the alerts as they happen.Practical complications also exist. Damaged, obscured or hard to read number plates can affect camera-based identification. Records of vehicles registered outside of Delhi may be incomplete or outdated. Authorities need to have a reliable way of checking these vehicles without increasing the level of congestion at the checkpoints.Another challenge is the sheer number of ways in you can watch the major highways and arterial roads, but smaller roads and connecting stretches may be opportunities to get around the checkpoints. If the enforcement is focused on some high-profile spots, motorists could just find alternative routes into the city. It would also put traffic into residential areas and smaller roads, creating new congestion problems.Delhi and neighboring NCR authorities will have to coordinate equally. Data on vehicle registrations, emission certificates and enforcement should be accessible across the states. Without smooth coordination, vehicles turned away at one checkpoint might try to enter via another route. The exercise would be more effective if there is a common enforcement mechanism across the NCR.The restrictions also have the potential to confuse daily commuters, especially those who travel to Delhi for work, education and business. Authorities will need to clearly communicate which vehicles are allowed, what documents drivers need to carry and how exemptions, if any, will be handled. It is equally important to ensure that enforcement is not arbitrary and that motorists do not face unnecessary delays or disputes at the checkpoints.The larger question is whether enforcement can be maintained for the three-month restriction period, from Nov. 1 to Jan. 31. There will be a lot of activity at the initial deployment and checks but the real test will be to see if the monitoring continues at the same intensity after the first few weeks.Authorities should also regularly publish data on the number of vehicles checked, turned away and penalized and details of enforcement at different entry points. Such disclosures would help to ascertain whether the restrictions are being uniformly applied, or whether there are any gaps.In the end, Delhi’s vehicle ban is only as good as its enforcement network. A rule that appears strict on paper will be of little use if thousands of vehicles continue to pass through the borders. The administration will need more than checkpoints and occasional drives, already stressed by winter pollution. It will require a coordinated, technology-enabled system that functions every day at every major point of entry.
Article Summary: Delhi is set to implement restrictions on older vehicles that fail to meet BS6 emission standards from entering the city. With potentially more than 10 lakh vehicles from neighboring NCR cities affected, the success of the move will depend on how effectively authorities are able to identify, intercept and turn away vehicles.

Article Title: Nimble fingers craft leisurely handmade suits in an age of mass-cloned garments
Article Text:
(Photo: Uma Kadam/TNN) MN Rao, a notable tailor in Mumbai, founded a successful tailoring house in 1965





MUMBAI: Way back in the 1960s, before actor AK Hangal became famous for his role as Rahim Chacha in 'Sholay', he was a master tailor in British cutting. Among the youngsters whom he mentored was one MN Rao, an enterprising migrant from Karnataka, who went on to launch his own tailoring store in Vile Parle in 1965.Years passed and Rao became a name to reckon with as far as hand-crafted bespoke menswear goes. From jackets, shirts, suits to sherwanis, Rao aced each style.Leading businessmen from Malabar Hill as well as politicians like Sushilkumar Shinde, CK Jaffer Sharief, Sharad Pawar and Ajit Panja sought customised outfits for special occasions.Now a new documentary 'MN Rao – Story of An Indian Tailor' by Shravan Ajay sheds light on the success of his 60-year-old tailoring house whose seamsters have worked here since 35-40 years. Each task is laboriously undertaken by hand -- from cutting and sewing to crafting buttonholes, pockets, seams, over days and weeks in an era when machinery can accomplish this in minutes.Subba Rao, Parvez Khan, Sugriv Kanojiya who hails from a village of istriwallahs in UP, Mohammed Idris Ansari and Mohd Naseem Siddiqui have spent decades over tables in this factory, cutting, sewing and ironing new outfits. Yet it is this very backbreaking meticulousness that deters the young generation from following in their footsteps.MN Rao passed away at age 52 in 1993. His two sons Vinayak and Madhusudan Rao continue his legacy. Madhusudan showed TOI around their Jogeshwari workshop where 40-odd karigars are paid handsomely, provided free WiFi and a fully AC environment, partly to avoid attrition.He said bespoke suits go a step beyond mere customised. "A bespoke garment is stitched for you and you alone using best, world class fabric and thread. We have a couple of meetings with the client, first for measurement, then fitting after cutting, and then we stitch it," Rao said.Many karigars specialize in whole garments like shirts, suits or jackets, some have honed one skill, either cutting, stitching or 'kaaj button' (buttonholes and buttons). One of the oldest employees of 35 years, Subba Rao narrated his journey as an apprentice who stitched buttons to now specialist.Chand Master, master cutter, trained in England with big international tailors in 1999. He said, "I returned to India because this is my home. I worked with major brands for over 30 years, and am here since 10 years."The cost of handmade garments runs into lakhs of rupees but high-end brands that use machines also charge similar amounts. Chand Master said, "Lekin haath toh haath hai. See Yusufbhai's fingers here. Real tailors' fingers become worn by carving buttonholes, and by sewing canvas on collars. The result is that your shirt may tear but the collar will not."Documentary maker Shravan Ajay said, "Chand Master was the life of my film. He would call, 'Cut! Cut!' I had to tell him, Chandbhai, your cut and my cut is different!"In a world where online retailers despatch mass-produced Ls and XLs in a day or two, the world of individual hand-crafted suits remains a timeless luxury.
Article Summary: MN Rao, a notable tailor in Mumbai, founded a successful tailoring house in 1965. A new documentary 'MN Rao – Story of An Indian Tailor' sheds light on the success of his 60-year-old house. The cost of handmade garments runs into lakhs of rupees.

Article Title: Alternative routes, night-time movement prescribed for sugar cane transport in Kolhapur
Article Text:
Kolhapur

:





With the sugarcane crushing season underway, Kolhapur police have introduced alternative routes for sugarcane transport vehicles to prevent traffic congestion and accidents in the city.Superintendent of police Nilotpal has appealed to transporters operating trucks, tractor-trolleys and bullock carts to strictly follow the routes prescribed by the City Traffic Branch. He has also directed that sugarcane transportation within the city be restricted to night hours, between 9pm and 6am.Police will also take action against tractor-trolleys operating without reflectors and those fitted with loudspeakers playing music at high volumes.“Many tractors transporting sugarcane are fitted with loudspeakers. The loud music prevents drivers from hearing horns sounded by vehicles approaching from behind. The use of such speakers has been banned. Reflectors must also be installed at the rear of every vehicle and bullock cart to ensure visibility and prevent accidents. Overloaded vehicles will also face penal action,” Nilotpal said.As per the guidelines issued by the City Traffic Branch, vehicles heading towards Chhatrapati Rajaram Sugar Factory from Tawde Hotel will proceed via Tararani Statue, Sadar Bazar Chowk, Dhairya Prasad Hall Chowk, SP Office Chowk and Kasba Bawda.Vehicles coming from Balinga will take the Phulewadi and Rankala Tower route.Vehicles arriving from Bhogawati and Kalamba will reach Kasba Bawda via Rankala Stand, Gangavesh, Shivaji Bridge, CPR Chowk and Mahavir College. An alternative route for vehicles from these areas will be via Puikhadi, New Vashi Naka, Ring Road, Kalamba, Sambhaji Nagar, CSIBER Chowk, Temblai Flyover, Tararani Statue and Sadar Bazar Chowk.Vehicles heading towards D Y Patil and Kumbhi sugar factories will pass through Tararani Statue, Sadar Bazar, Dhairya Prasad Hall, Ramanmala Post Office Chowk, Mahavir College, CPR Chowk, Shivaji Bridge, Gangavesh, Rankala Stand, Rankala Tower and Phulewadi.Vehicles travelling towards Bidri Sugar Factory via Tararani Statue will take the Temblai Flyover, Highway Canteen Chowk, CSIBER Chowk, Ring Road, Sambhaji Nagar and Kalamba route.Meanwhile, the route from Phulewadi Naka via Chiwa Bazar, Kalamba Hockey Stadium, CSIBER Chowk, Highway Canteen (KSBP Chowk), Koyasco Chowk, National Highway, Shiye and Kasba Bawda to Rajaram Sugar Factory will remain open for sugarcane transport round the clock. The Shiye-Bhuye-Wadange route to Dalmia Sugar Factory will also remain open 24 hours.
Article Summary: Kolhapur police introduce alternative routes for sugarcane transport vehicles to prevent traffic congestion and accidents. Sugarcane transportation within the city be restricted to night hours, between 9pm and 6am. Police will also take action against tractor-trolleys operating without reflectors and those fitted with loudspeakers playing music at high volumes.

Article Title: Mumbai-bound traffic hit after hatchback catches fire on Vashi Creek bridge
Article Text:
The driver immediately pulled the car over to the roadside after noticing smoke emanating from the engine.





NAVI MUMBAI: Vehicular traffic from Navi Mumbai towards Mumbai was disrupted for around 30 minutes after a hatchback caught fire while crossing the Vashi Creek Bridge on Friday at around 7.30pm.The driver escaped unhurt. He immediately pulled the car over to the roadside after noticing smoke emanating from the engine. However, the fire soon engulfed the entire vehicle, leaving it completely charred.Vashi traffic police alerted the Vashi fire brigade, which reached the spot within 15 minutes. The charred vehicle was later towed away by a crane, following which traffic movement returned to normal.Sunil Kadam, senior inspector of the Vashi traffic unit, said the driver was identified as Sumit Bhikaji Kadam.“At around 7.45pm, we received a call from one Rahul, whose full name is not known, informing us that a car had caught fire on the Mumbai-bound lane of the Vashi Creek Bridge,” said AV Sisode, the on-duty fireman at Vashi fire station.“In the meantime, we also received a call from the Vashi traffic police and immediately rushed to the spot with a fire tender. The Mumbai fire brigade team had also reached the spot as there was some confusion over the jurisdiction,” Sisode said.The fire was subsequently extinguished, and the Vashi fire brigade team returned to the station at around 8.30pm.
Article Summary: The driver immediately pulled the car over to the roadside after noticing smoke emanating from the engine. The fire soon engulfed the entire vehicle, leaving it completely charred. The charred vehicle was later towed away by a crane, following which traffic movement returned to normal.

Article Title: Paes to run for AITA vice-president
Article Text: Pune: In a move filled with surprise and intrigue, Leander Paes has decided to run for the lone vice-president’s post in the All India Tennis Association (AITA) elections, scheduled for Nov 27.The 18-time Grand Slam winner’s candidature was revealed by Chintan Parikh, AITA’s interim president, in a press release on Sunday.Parikh said his partnership with Paes, who is the president of the Bengal Tennis Association, was finalised after a meeting between the two in Kolkata on Friday.“Parikh will contest as president and Paes as vice president. Both of them will be supported by a capable team of honorary secretary, treasurer, two joint secretaries and other Executive Committee members ... these names will be decided in the next few days,” the press release said.“Both of them have agreed to commit themselves to the mission named ‘Tennis First’ that aims at clean and transparent governance in AITA, adherence to code of ethics as per ITF guidelines ... and ultimately preparing the nation with a world-class tennis ecosystem by 2030”.As per the National Sports Governance Act, 2025, a candidate must have completed at least one term as an office-bearer in a state association or on the executive committee of the national body to be eligible to run for president.Paes was elected to the BTA top job last November.He could have run for AITA president as a Sportsperson of Outstanding Merit, but he refrained from filing for nomination, despite being the only Olympic medal winner in the roster.Mahesh Bhupathi and Sania Mirza, the other two Grand Slam winners in the SOM roster, have filed their nominations.Rohan Bopanna, the other major winner, had applied to be on the SOM roster, but was ruled ineligible as he had not completed the one-year cooling period since he played his last professional tournament, in October 2025.
Article Summary: Leander Paes has decided to run for the lone vice-president’s post in the All India Tennis Association (AITA) elections, scheduled for Nov 27. The 18-time Grand Slam winner's candidature was revealed by Chintan Parikh, AITA's interim president, on Sunday.

Article Title: Friend arrested for assaulting autorickshaw driver to death
Article Text:
Pune:





A 30-year-old autorickshaw driver was allegedly murdered after his friend hit him on the head with a stone following a minor altercation in Kasewadi, Bhawani Peth, on Friday night.Khadak police have arrested the accused, Amol Anil Ambwane (26), a resident of Kasewadi, in connection with the murder.“We arrested Ambwane for assaulting Aslam Yusuf Khan (30) on the head with a stone following a minor altercation,” said senior inspector Dhananjay Pingale of Khadak police.The deceased’s elder brother, Muzzammil (33), lodged a complaint with the Khadak police.“Ambwane and Khan were friends. Around 11.30pm, Khan was leaving Kasewadi when Ambwane stopped him and picked a quarrel with him over a trivial issue. Both exchanged abuses, following which Ambwane picked up a paver block and hit Khan on the head. Khan’s friend, who was passing by the spot, witnessed the incident and alerted Muzzammil,” Pingale said.He said there were no visible external injuries. “Khan and his brother returned home, but Khan soon started feeling dizzy,” he added.“After reaching home, Khan went to sleep. His family members tried to wake him up, but he did not respond. They rushed him to a hospital, where doctors declared him dead on arrival,” Pingale said.A subsequent examination revealed that Khan had died due to internal head injuries.“Our team then searched for Ambwane in the area and nabbed him,” Pingale said.
Article Summary: A 30-year-old autorickshaw driver was allegedly murdered after his friend hit him on the head with a stone following a minor altercation. Amol Anil Ambwane (26), a resident of Kasewadi, was arrested in connection with the murder.

Article Title: Diwali Pahat balances tradition with a bid to woo younger audiences
Article Text:
Viraj Joshi, grandson of Bhimsen Joshi, to perform at various venues throughout Diwali week

Pune:





At the break of dawn when Maharashtra welcomes Diwali, Indian raga sangeet, devotional abhangs and lighter melodies bring together people from all walks of life. The Diwali Pahat tradition, which took shape in Pune in the early 1990s in Pune, is evolving as organisers experiment with formats and festive attractions to draw younger crowds while musicians preserve its core: morning ragas performed at the hour they belong to.“For me, music is a thread that brings a family together. My father is my guru, and performing in Pune during Diwali, with my family around, is always special,” said vocalist Viraj Joshi, whose father, Srinivas Joshi, is also performing in the city this season. Viraj’s schedule includes performances in Delhi, Solapur, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar and Pune.He remains committed to a classical foundation. “Audiences always want to hear the abhangs and traditions of my grandfather pandit Bhimsen Joshi , and I make it a point to begin my concerts with a raga. I include several morning ragas because this is one of the few occasions when audiences get to hear them performed,” he said.Srinivas Joshi, Viraj’s father said Diwali Pahat was perhaps the only occasion for artistes to perform at that hour and share morning ragas. “I cherish the tradition of beginning Diwali with an uplifting classical music concert. It’s an important way to begin the festival personally too as I get to celebrate with my musical and extended family of listeners.Organisers, meanwhile, are finding ways to broaden the experience.At the Ritwik Foundation for Performing Arts, this year’s Swar Prabhat on Nov 1 featured Jaipur-Atrauli gharana exponent Shruti Sadolikar in a full-length morning recital, accompanied by tabla player Abhay Datar and harmonium player Anant Joshi.“Usually, we have two artistes sharing a concert. This time, we wanted to give one artiste the space for a full-length morning mehfil,” said Shruti Porwal of the foundation. She said 35-40% of registrations came from new audiences. The organisation is seeking younger listeners, and the recorded recital will be uploaded on YouTube during Diwali.At Pune International Centre (PIC), the Oct 31-Nov 1 programme took the celebration beyond the concert stage. Alongside vocalist Shruti Vishwakarma Marathe’s performance, accompanied by Pranav Gurav on tabla and Leeladhar Chakradev on harmonium, an exhibition brought together local vendors selling pottery, ceramics, faral, chocolates and handmade products.PIC co-convener for art and culture Jui Tawade said its first Diwali Pahat aimed to combine local Diwali businesses with a concert and offer residents of surrounding areas, including Panchavati, a cultural gathering closer to home.The musical canvas will also extend to instrumental collaborations, with flautist Rakesh Chaurasia and Mohan veena exponent Vishwa Mohan Bhatt scheduled to perform together on Nov 6 at Phoenix Avenue of Stars in Viman Nagar.NIBM Road resident Piyush Mehta, who discovered Diwali Pahat after moving to Pune in 2015, said attending with parents and children had become a tradition. Concerts began across the city last week and will continue through Diwali week.
Article Summary: The Diwali Pahat tradition took shape in Pune in the early 1990s. Organisers experiment with formats and festive attractions to draw younger crowds. Concerts began across the city last week and will continue through DiWali week.

Article Title: Cong celebrated MLC poll win amid drought, says Bawankule
Article Text:
Revenue minister Chandrashekhar Bawankule with mayor Neeta Thakre and other functionaries addressed media on BJP’s nationwide campaign to save democracy on Sunday

Nagpur:





Revenue minister Chandrashekhar Bawankule on Sunday alleged that Congress lured voters for Nagpur Graduates Constituency polls through “mutton parties” and later celebrated its win lavishly even as “farmers are facing drought”.The minister questioned how Congress can spend on unnecessary things while seeking additional help for farmers. “They talk about drought relief and throw mutton parties. After they won the seat, their celebrations were over-the-top. Congress members could have gone home quietly after victory became official,” said Bawankule.He also said Congress winning the MLC seat is not a big deal. “They have merely retained the seat. It would have assumed significance had they wrested the seat, like in 2020,” he said.The revenue minister added that Congress was always a second choice, but won on a technicality. “BJP came first on first-preference votes. Congress won by taking second-preference votes. All the anti-BJP candidates on the ballot paper gave their second preference to Congress. Still, we have to accept the result and move on,” he said.Dismissing the charge that a weak candidate cost BJP the seat, Bawankule defended Sudhakar Kohale, a former city BJP president and two-time MLA. “Looking at the number of votes he got. If Kohale was the wrong candidate, how did 64,000 voted for him?” he asked.Justifying Special Intensive Revision (SIR) across the country, Bawankule linked the low turnout to bloated rolls. “In Nagpur alone, there are 2 lakh to 2.5 lakh duplicate names and as many dead voters. Why do only 60% vote and not 100%? Names have been added to the list since 2002, but none have been deleted,” he said.Citing the example of Kamptee assembly constituency represented by him, the minister said voters have names in Kamptee, in Hudkeshwar and also in Jaiprakash Nagar. “People vote in a nagar panchayat and then come and vote in the municipal corporation. One person should vote only once,” said Bawankule.The minister accused Congress of winning through bogus voting. “This will become a thing of the past, because the coming voter list will be accurate,” he said.
Article Summary: Revenue minister Chandrashekhar Bawankule alleged that Congress lured voters for Nagpur Graduates Constituency polls through ‘mutton parties’ He also said Congress winning the MLC seat is not a big deal. “They talk about drought relief and throw mutton parties. After they won the seat, their celebrations were over- the-top,” he said.

Article Title: Oscar-winning sound designer to work on Futala acoustic next week
Article Text:
Resul Pookutty

Nagpur:





Whether a visitor takes a seat or walks from one end of Futala’s viewing gallery to the other, the music should sound equally clear, without any noticeable rise or drop in volume. That is the acoustic experience Oscar-winning sound designer Resul Pookutty will work towards when he visits Nagpur next week, as the musical fountain’s restoration enters its final technical phase.With official programming beginning this month, the international technical team has started configuring the fountain’s multimedia systems. The exercise will be followed by audio tuning and, subsequently, synchronisation of the water jets and lighting effects over a period of a month.Emmy Award-winning cinematographer and Futala’s technical director Alphonse Roy told TOI that Pookutty’s role goes far beyond conventional sound design. He will fine-tune the audio system to ensure consistent sound quality throughout the viewing gallery, regardless of where spectators stand or move.Roy said that Pookutty travelled to Las Vegas to study how audio systems were designed for large-scale entertainment installations. Drawing on those observations and Futala’s unique outdoor acoustic requirements, he subsequently approached Dolby to have its algorithm rewritten to suit the installation.The objective is to eliminate noticeable fluctuations in sound as visitors move across the gallery, creating a seamless listening experience despite the challenges posed by an open-air setting.“Unlike an enclosed auditorium, Futala has no walls or ceiling to contain sound. Wind, atmospheric conditions and the distance between speakers and spectators make precise audio calibration particularly challenging,” senior officials said.Meanwhile, the programming exercise will establish the sequences through which the fountain’s mechanical and electronic systems operate together. Once audio tuning is completed, attention will shift towards coordinating the programmed water movements with lighting and sound.The development follows last Sunday’s brief display, when water jets and orange lights came alive for a few minutes, offering a glimpse of the restoration’s progress. The international team, including Belgian expert Basile de Schrynmakers and Nicholas, is currently in Nagpur for the final preparations.MahaMetro officials remain confident of achieving technical readiness by the first week of December. However, the formal inauguration and commencement of public shows will depend on necessary approvals.For Futala, the final challenge is no longer merely making the water dance, but ensuring that every sound, light and movement performs in harmony.
Article Summary: Resul Pookutty will fine-tune the audio system to ensure consistent sound quality. The objective is to eliminate noticeable fluctuations in sound as visitors move across the gallery. Once audio tuning is completed, attention will shift towards coordinating the programmed water movements with lighting and sound.
